summary: The full methodology for FLIPR, the 2026 Silver Bulletin House, Senate and governor model, descended from Silver's 2010 FiveThirtyEight midterm model and refit in 2018 and 2022. It sets out seven steps. (1) Polling averages with house effects, partisan-poll priors, a likely-voter adjustment and a generic-ballot timeline adjustment. (2) A national environment blending the generic ballot with a bottom-up estimate from race polls, plus CANTOR similarity scores to impute Lite estimates. (3) Classic: simple fundamentals (partisan lean plus generic ballot) and regression-based 'fancy fundamentals', mixed according to polarization. (4) Deluxe: de-biased expert ratings with reduced weight. (5) Nudging the snapshot toward a historical prior. (6) Layered uncertainty: national drift, Election Day error, statewide, race-level and correlated demographic error. (7) 40,000 simulations with fat tails, ranked-choice voting, runoffs, independents and turnout. The article ends with an exhaustive list of 2026 changes.

findings.statement: FLIPR forecasts House, Senate and governor races and is trained on both midterm and presidential years. Some of its code dates to Silver's first midterm forecast at FiveThirtyEight in 2010; it was nearly completely refit in 2018, when Lite/Classic/Deluxe was introduced, changed again in 2022 to reflect polarization, and every line of the 2022 code was audited and often improved for 2026 with help from AI coding tools. No congressional forecast was run in 2024.
findings.rationale: Changes execute the original design with more precision, robustness and internal consistency rather than changing its philosophy.
findings.evidence_quote: The model underwent a near-complete refit in 2018 when the Lite/Classic/Deluxe concept was introduced.

findings.statement: FLIPR stacks three layers, each defining a version: Lite derives as much as possible from polls alone; Classic adds non-polling leading indicators ('fundamentals'); Deluxe adds expert race ratings. Deluxe is the default, and expert ratings are described as the least important layer.
findings.evidence_quote: Lite derives as much information as possible from polls alone;

findings.statement: FLIPR runs 40,000 simulations every time the model is updated and uses variance-reduction techniques so the effective sample size is larger than 40,000.
findings.rationale: Simulations are needed because of complex correlations between races.
findings.evidence_quote: we run 40,000 simulations every time the model is updated.

findings.statement: For 2026, FLIPR increases the relative weight on fundamentals versus polls because elections have become more predictable from partisanship with less ticket-splitting, while polls have had some rough years. It also accounts for the national environment 'locking in' earlier, so the generic ballot is more predictive months ahead than it once was.
findings.evidence_quote: should our model increase the relative weight on “fundamentals” as opposed to polls? The answer is basically yes

findings.statement: FLIPR is fit primarily on Senate races since 1990 and on House and gubernatorial races since 1998.
findings.evidence_quote: The model is fit primarily based on Senate races since 1990, and House and gubernatorial races since 1998.

findings.statement: Unlike the presidential model, which defaults toward polls-only by Election Day, FLIPR is a more even blend of polls and fundamentals even at the end, because non-polling data is richer for about 500 races and polling is sparse, with many House races getting little or no nonpartisan polling.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR is more of an even blend between polls and fundamentals

findings.statement: FLIPR distinguishes 'micro' indicators that apply to one race (race polls, candidate fundraising) from 'macro' indicators that affect all races (generic ballot, polarization). Races cannot be forecast independently and then simulated, because outcomes are correlated, as in 2016 when Republicans beat their polls across the board.
findings.rationale: Systematic error versus independent race variance.
findings.evidence_quote: You can’t just forecast each race individually and apply some sort of Monte Carlo simulation on top because race outcomes are somewhat correlated.

findings.statement: Step 1: FLIPR's race-level polling averages use the shared Silver Bulletin algorithm. Polls are weighted by recency, sample size and pollster rating, adjusted for house effects, and smoothed by averaging more aggressive and more conservative LOWESS regression curves.
findings.evidence_quote: we’ve found the best way to do this is to calculate what are essentially various LOWESS regression curves, and then average more aggressive and more conservative versions.

findings.statement: FLIPR's house effects are estimated from both generic ballot and individual race polls, and are more punitive to partisan or internal campaign polls released publicly, which start with a prior that they are biased. Historically that bias averages about 4 points toward the preferred candidate.
findings.evidence_quote: On average in the historical data, this bias is about 4 points toward their preferred candidate.

findings.statement: FLIPR adjusts every registered-voter or all-adult poll toward what it would show among likely voters, estimated from surveys that publish both versions. The shift is shrunk toward a prior until enough paired polls exist to phase the prior out. In 2026 most paired surveys favored Democrats in the LV version.
findings.evidence_quote: the magnitude of the shift is shrunken toward a prior

findings.statement: FLIPR dropped its old prior that the RV-to-LV shift favors Republicans, because Democrats' college-educated coalition now turns out at high rates. It uses a more neutral prior that is overridden more quickly as paired LV/RV polls arrive.
findings.evidence_quote: the model has discarded its prior that the shift from registered voters to likely voters typically favors Republicans.

findings.statement: FLIPR applies a timeline adjustment: if the generic ballot has moved since a race was last polled, a fraction of that movement is added to the race's margin, since a partial correction works better than a full one empirically. Race averages can therefore shift without new polls.
findings.evidence_quote: We’ve found empirically that a partial correction works better than a full correction.

findings.statement: FLIPR also applies the likely-voter adjustment to its own versions of the generic ballot and presidential approval, which Silver Bulletin's regular averages do not. In early August 2026 this moved the generic ballot from about D+6.5 to about D+8.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR also applies the likely voter adjustment to its averages of the generic ballot and presidential approval, which our regular averages do not.

findings.statement: Presidential approval averages tolerate more aggressive smoothing settings, while the generic ballot average must be fairly conservative or it bounces around too much; Silver says he tried it the other way.
findings.evidence_quote: the generic ballot average needs to be fairly conservative or will bounce around too much

findings.statement: Step 2: FLIPR estimates the national environment as a weighted average of the generic ballot and a 'bottom-up' estimate implied by polls of individual Senate and House races relative to each race's partisan lean. Weights depend on the relative amount of generic ballot versus race polling. Gubernatorial polls are excluded from this calculation because they correlate less with state partisanship. Example: generic ballot D+8 and race polls implying D+4 give about D+6.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR will basically take an average of these

findings.statement: New in 2026, the bottom-up national estimate gives more weight to states and districts that resemble most others nationally, so a poll of a Pennsylvania swing district counts more than one in Hawaii or rural Alabama. It also corrects for selection bias in which races get polled.
findings.rationale: Competitive-looking races in lopsided seats get polled more, which biases naive estimates.
findings.evidence_quote: a poll of a swing district in Pennsylvania will have more impact on the calculation than a race in Hawaii or rural Alabama.

findings.statement: Partisan lean scores for each state and district are based on the past two presidential elections relative to the nation and on recent state legislative elections, and reflect new boundaries after redistricting. They are denominated in margin: R+10 means 10 points more Republican in margin than the nation, which Cook PVI would call R+5 because PVI uses one party's vote share. Texas was about R+11 in 2026.
findings.evidence_quote: If we say a district is R +10, that means the vote margin in that district is 10 points more Republican than in the country overall.

findings.statement: Elasticity, each state's or district's sensitivity to national swings, is estimated from Cooperative Election Study voter-level microdata for 2016 through 2025. It is applied at various points in FLIPR, including scaling national error shifts, but mostly has a minor impact.
findings.evidence_quote: This elasticity calculation, which is derived from voter-level microdata

findings.statement: CANTOR (Congressional Algorithm using Neighboring Typologies to Optimize Regression) computes pairwise similarity scores among all 485 units, 435 districts plus 50 states. It uses political traits (partisan lean), demographics (race, religion, education) and geography (region with Silver's own definitions and some split states, distance, urbanization). It then imputes polling-like estimates for unpolled races from how polls in similar places over- or under-perform their baselines.
findings.rationale: Overperformance tends to cluster in similar places.
findings.evidence_quote: it calculates similarity scores between any given combination of states or districts

findings.statement: For 2026, CANTOR accounts for a wider array of demographics, notably separating religious groups such as Jewish and Muslim voters that were previously lumped with others.
findings.evidence_quote: A wider array of demographics are now accounted for by CANTOR, particularly including religious groups

findings.statement: Step 3: FLIPR computes two fundamentals estimates. 'Simple fundamentals' are the generic ballot plus partisan lean. 'Fancy fundamentals' come from a large regression on races since 1990 including candidate-quality factors. Before 2022 only fancy fundamentals were used. For congressional races, simple fundamentals now get almost half the weight in many cases, implying candidate-quality factors including incumbency are about half as important as over the period since 1990.
findings.rationale: Polarization crowds out everything but partisanship.
findings.evidence_quote: For Congressional races, “simple fundamentals” now get almost half the weight in many cases.

findings.statement: The ratio of simple to fancy fundamentals is now tied to a polarization coefficient instead of a fixed ratio. Polarization is measured as the difference in party means from Voteview. Fancy fundamentals now use FLIPR's full national-environment estimate; simple fundamentals use the generic ballot alone.
findings.evidence_quote: Our indicator for polarization is the difference in party means from Voteview.

findings.statement: New in 2026: when simple and fancy fundamentals disagree, as for popular Republican Gov. Phil Scott in Vermont, FLIPR trusts fundamentals less, puts more weight on polls and expert ratings, and increases the race's uncertainty. When they agree, it increases the weight on fundamentals.
findings.evidence_quote: In cases where “simple fundamentals” and “fancy fundamentals” are not aligned, the model trusts fundamentals less in general.

findings.statement: Fancy fundamentals fit separate regressions for incumbent and open-seat races; races with appointed incumbents count as open seats. Incumbency handling uses congressional approval polls to gauge the climate for incumbents, a larger incumbency advantage in small or idiosyncratic states and districts with low CANTOR similarity, the incumbent's margin in their last competitive race adjusted for that year's environment and redistricting, whether the incumbent is in a first elected term or beat an incumbent last time (both treated as strengths), and a smaller advantage when new and old districts overlap little.
findings.rationale: First-termers lacked incumbency last time, so their last margin understates strength.
findings.evidence_quote: we technically fit separate regressions for incumbent and open-seat races.

findings.statement: Fancy fundamentals include fundraising from individual contributions only, excluding party and PAC money, with in-state contributions weighted 5x. They also include elected experience on a 0-3 scale, from never elected to current or former senator or governor; party-loyalty scores from congressional votes for incumbents only, since defectors outperform; and scandals, with new scandals counting more than ones a candidate has already survived. The scandal list was compiled by Nathaniel Rakich and is one of the more subjective parts of the model.
findings.evidence_quote: Home-state contributions get a 5x weight.

findings.statement: FLIPR now estimates the in-state share of contributions from donors whose state is known and extrapolates it to all individual contributions, including small-donor money the FEC does not itemize by state, fixing a clumsy 2022 implementation. Late replacement candidates and candidates who eschew individual contributions, such as JB Pritzker, now have fundraising treated as missing and estimated by proxy instead of zero; FLIPR does not account for self-funding.
findings.evidence_quote: Because FLIPR does not account for self-funding, these candidates would previously have been treated as raising zero money

findings.statement: Classic uses a small weight on CANTOR's imputed polling proxies, because CANTOR is generally less accurate than either fundamentals or actual race polls.
findings.evidence_quote: While CANTOR is a cool system, it’s generally less accurate than either fundamentals or polls directly from the state or district.

findings.statement: In recent elections the Deluxe forecast typically calls only one or two additional races correctly out of about 500 compared with Classic. Expert ratings are good at ranking races relative to each other but persistently assume a neutral national environment (generic ballot near zero) until late in the cycle: in early August 2026 they implied about D+2 versus FLIPR Classic's D+7.

quantities.name: extra correct calls, Deluxe vs Classic

findings.evidence_quote: expert raters tend to implicitly assume a neutral political environment (i.e., a generic ballot of about zero) until quite late in the cycle.

findings.statement: Step 4 (Deluxe): (1) translate ratings from Cook Political Report, Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball into implied margins, using a Bayesian treatment for Solid/Safe ratings, which are informative only when Classic puts the race near a category boundary; (2) estimate each outlet's implied national environment; (3) shift the ratings to FLIPR's national environment to de-bias them; (4) blend with Classic.
findings.rationale: Experts' value is in rank-ordering races, not in the national environment.
findings.evidence_quote: De-bias the expert ratings by shifting them to FLIPR’s estimate of the national environment.

findings.statement: Expert ratings now get about one-sixth of the forecast for polled congressional races and about one-quarter for polled governor races, with more weight in unpolled races and wherever FLIPR judges fundamentals and polls less reliable. Previously they got about one-third across the board.
findings.rationale: Use experts as a fallback where other indicators are unreliable.
findings.evidence_quote: It’s typically about one-sixth of the forecast for Congressional races with polling and one-quarter of the forecast for gubernatorial races with polling

findings.statement: The 2026 code audit found that earlier de-biasing of expert ratings leaked some of the experts' neutral-environment assumption into Deluxe; FLIPR now removes that bias completely so experts cannot affect the national picture.
findings.evidence_quote: there was a bit of leakage from the experts’ implicit assumptions about the national environment

findings.statement: Step 5: a prior for the House popular vote is fit on macro factors since 1946: presidential approval, the previous House popular vote adjusted for uncontested 'blank districts', polarization, and midterm status. Classic and Deluxe nudge the current snapshot toward this prior, with an effect that is gentle and fades to zero by Election Day; Lite uses the snapshot with wider uncertainty. In August 2026 the prior was about D+8.5 versus a snapshot near D+7.
findings.rationale: As the generic ballot became more stable, the prior is less useful than it used to be.
findings.evidence_quote: the effect of this adjustment is relatively gentle, and essentially fades out by Election Day.

findings.statement: FLIPR's prior now distinguishes presidential years from midterms more sharply, because midterms tend to produce more lopsided outcomes.
findings.evidence_quote: Midterms tend to produce more lopsided outcomes than are typically seen in congressional elections in presidential years.

findings.statement: Illustration of FLIPR's uncertainty logic: a candidate leading by 3 points with a 5-point margin of error wins 88 percent of the time; if the margin of error doubles to 10 points, 72 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: A candidate with a 3-point lead in a race where the margin of error is 5 points will win her race 88 percent of the time.

findings.statement: Step 6: race-level uncertainty in FLIPR is higher when there is less polling, more undecided voters, more time until the election, and more disagreement between model subcomponents such as fundamentals versus polls. Primary polls often miss by double digits.
findings.rationale: The degree of uncertainty is itself predictable.
findings.evidence_quote: There’s more time to go until the election;

findings.statement: FLIPR splits error into layers. National error shifts all races together, scaled by each unit's elasticity, and has two parts: 'drift', the change in the national environment before Election Day, which is smaller under high polarization and goes to zero by Election Day, and Election Day systematic polling error. Local error has a statewide draw shared by all races in a state (new in 2026) and a race-specific draw. Correlated demographic error uses CANTOR's variables to simulate over- or underperformance among subgroups such as Hispanics, Catholics or the Northeast, producing clustered regional errors like those of 2018 and 2022.
findings.rationale: Errors are more correlated across similar places.
findings.evidence_quote: Finally, correlated demographic error is an intermediate layer that sits between these and is the most complex layer.

findings.statement: FLIPR now calibrates drift separately from Election Day error, where it previously blended them; the new specification is more consistent with the presidential forecast. The recalibration showed the national picture locks in earlier than it used to.
findings.evidence_quote: Previously, the model blended drift and Election Day uncertainty together.

findings.statement: FLIPR now assumes congressional and gubernatorial races are slightly more correlated with one another in presidential years than in midterms, because the presidential race anchors everything.
findings.evidence_quote: The model now assumes that races are slightly more correlated with one another in presidential years than they are in midterms.

findings.statement: Step 7: FLIPR's simulations use slightly fat-tailed distributions for rare out-of-sample events, but the fat tails are less severe than in past years because recent cycles lacked huge outliers.
findings.evidence_quote: Fat tails are less severe than in past years, as we now have more cycles without huge outlier outcomes.

findings.statement: For races with prominent independent candidates, FLIPR simulates the independent's vote share with a right-tailed distribution: usually not close, with an outside chance of real momentum. Independents who are de facto partisans, such as Dan Osborn in Nebraska or Bernie Sanders, are treated as members of that party.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR simulates the independent’s vote share using a right-tailed statistical distribution

findings.statement: FLIPR's simulations handle ranked-choice voting in Maine and Alaska, Alaska's top-four primary, Georgia-style runoffs when no candidate reaches 50 percent, and Louisiana's House jungle primary, used for the last time in 2026.
findings.evidence_quote: In states like Georgia where elections go to runoffs if no candidate gets 50 percent of the vote, FLIPR simulates this too;

findings.statement: FLIPR simulates turnout probabilistically as a post-processing step that does not affect vote shares or win probabilities. Local turnout is benchmarked on race competitiveness, whether a Senate or governor race is on the ballot, past turnout, and estimated voting-eligible population adjusted for growth. National turnout comes from polls asking whether voters are more or less excited than usual. Turnout within a state must be consistent across House, Senate and governor races within bounds, gets a capped correction for differential party turnout, and district totals are scaled to match the authoritative national estimate.
findings.evidence_quote: The turnout simulations are essentially a post-processing step

findings.statement: FLIPR treats gubernatorial races as less partisan than congressional races more completely in 2026: fundamentals are considerably upweighted for congressional forecasts and slightly downweighted for governors relative to the 2022 build, because partisan lean and fundraising data are less reliable for governor races.
findings.evidence_quote: fundamentals are considerably upweighted in our congressional forecasts but slightly downweighted for governors.

findings.statement: FLIPR now calculates its own native presidential approval rating with a likely-voter adjustment.
findings.evidence_quote: The model now calculates its own native version of presidential approval ratings that makes a likely-voter adjustment.

political_insights.insight: Party means in congressional voting (Voteview) have kept diverging, so the parties now vote as unified blocks with almost no crossover, and election outcomes increasingly follow partisanship.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Scale the weight on partisan lean versus candidate factors with a polarization index.

political_insights.insight: Gubernatorial races still feature much more ticket-splitting than congressional races, for example Republican Phil Scott in Vermont.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Use weaker partisan priors and wider uncertainty for governor races.

political_insights.insight: The 2018 midterm had pockets of Republican strength (Florida, rural Senate states) and 2022 had a mini red wave in New York and New Jersey.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model regional and demographic correlated errors, not just national swing.

references.description: Voteview congressional polarization data (difference in party means)
Cooperative Election Study 2016-2025 microdata for elasticity
Nathaniel Rakich's scandal list, maintained by Silver Bulletin
Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball race ratings

open_questions: Exact regression coefficients of the fancy-fundamentals model and how they vary with polarization.
How CANTOR similarity weights are computed and how its selection-bias correction works.
Variance parameters for drift, Election Day error, statewide, local and demographic layers.
Shape of the fat-tailed distribution and the variance-reduction technique used.
Mapping of expert rating categories to margins, and the Bayesian handling of Solid ratings.
